Yeah, what's good, is that he sells it with an ECU, gearbox, mounts and everything (I think the only bigger part I'll need to handle on my own is the exhaust).

He's rebuilt it for his Civic, which he (claims) that he totalled later. I have no way to verify it, though. A borked rebuild might be another reason why he's selling it... JDM B18C are rare as hell.

Personally, I would stay far away from any engine that an amateur "rebuilt" himself, and instead look for either a good used engine in a salvage yard that you can hear run, with a warranty, or a factory remanufactured engine such as a Jasper that comes with a long term parts and labor warranty.

Believe it or not, it is actually cheaper to remanufacture an engine in a factory setting than it is to do it at home or even in a professional repair shop; there is a lot of very expensive and time consuming machine work and measuring involved that requires some very expensive specialized equipment and training to operate.. That is why you very rarely see any repair garage that rebuilds engines in house these days, although it was common a generation ago. When I hear "rebuilt it myself" in connection with an engine, it makes the hair on the back of my neck stand up. Typically what that means is that someone who may not even own a torque wrench took the engine apart, put some new gaskets and bearing inserts in it without measuring anything or having parts machined back into tolerance, and then slapped it all back together. Usually this means the cylinders were not bored, crankshaft was not turned, no line boring was done, no pressure testing and magnafluxing for internal cracks, no hot tank dip to remove internal contamination, no ring end gap measurements/ grinding, no valve job; none of the things that bring a worn engine back into the mechanical tolerances it was built with. Typically an engine that was "rebuilt" for significantly less than what a factory rebuilt one costs is not done correctly, and usually will not last very long.

Myself, i have been a professional mechanic for 35+ years at the same busy shop. Years ago I used to do a lot of engine building, and this always involved sending the parts out to a machine shop at a typical cost of $1000 to $1500 depending on how much work was needed before we could rebuild it in house (and that was just for the outside machinist work back in the 1980's and 90's). The last engine I built in our shop was about 15 years ago; around that time installing a factory remanufactured one actually became cheaper, with a 50,000 mile parts and labor warranty from the manufacturer.

Obviously there are stylistic conventions concerning questions in writing (such as ending them with a question mark). Equally obviously there can be grammatical constructs which are inherent to questions (e.g. we say, "These are dogs.", but invert the word order to ask, "Are these dogs?"). But is this all there is to a question, and would you say that a question is in the province of grammar? Or, considering inflection can be an integral element of a question (e.g. "These are dogs." vs "These are dogs?"), is a question related more to tense? And is tense separate and superordinate to grammar?
[Serious] In linguistics, what constitutes a question and what rules govern it?

Are you asking about linguistics in general or specifically about English? Because the rules are strongly language-dependent. For example, in some languages inflection is the only way to tell apart a statement from a question (romance languages such as Spanish and Italian are like that, so in writing the presence of a question mark or other symbol is essential). In others questions are characterized by (typically) having interrogative particles in it: Latin and Japanese are examples of this.
